I said that so far as I could recall, the statement concerning thirty ships having been sunk was made by a member of this house-I am not sure as to that, but if not it was made by a public man of some sort or other. I do not know whether he was a member of a legislature; at all events he occupied some sort of public position; he was in the public eye. In reply to that statement, I declared that the number sunk was twenty. It seems necessary to continue to make these denials indefinitely.
Going on a little further, Mr. Gagnon is quoted in the press as having said that on one day, September 10, five ships were sunk in this area. In that statement Mr. Gagnon is absolutely wrong. There is no record of five ships having been sunk in the river on that date.
Mr. Gagnon is further quoted as saying that two United States destroyers were sunk, presumably in the same area. In reply to that statement I can say that there is no record of any American destroyers having been sunk at any time in this area.
Mr. Gagnon says that he has a list of the names of the ships sunk and the dates on which they were sunk. I asked Mr. Gagnon to produce this list for my investigation. I have asked him by telegram and he replied that surely my own department has the information. My department cannot have this information on ghost ships having been sunk- flying Dutchmen or something of that sort. My department has information as to the sinking of twenty ships, and I have told Mr. Gagnon that if he has information to the contrary and makes statements to the contrary, it is his duty to make good those

Canadian Navy-Sinkings in St. Lawrence
statements. Every time I have made the statement as to twenty ships having been sunk I relied for my information upon the records of the Department of Naval Service. I may say that twenty may be a high figure, because included in the twenty are at least two ships which might properly be said to have been sunk outside the gulf area proper.
Mr. Gagnon goes on to say that control from Ottawa is responsible for delay in attacking the submarines after they have been sighted. I say definitely that so far as the naval service is concerned any naval ship sighting an enemy submarine anywhere would attack instantly without awaiting instructions from anybody, because that is what they are there for. I say further that the general control of these matters is in the hands of the naval officer in charge either at Gaspe or Quebec or Halifax, and no direction or concurrence from Ottawa is needed to carry out an attack.
Mr. Gagnon also makes a reference to the Royal Canadian Air Force, which he criticizes in somewhat the same terms. I believe that what I have said about the naval ships would apply with equal correctness to the air force. In any case I think the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) some time ago dealt adequately with a charge of this sort.
In the debate in the legislature last week some reference was made to the fact that there might be refuelling bases in the river and gulf of St. Lawrence for enemy submarines. All I can say to that is that no trace of any such bases has ever been discovered although most thorough investigations have been made. Any one who reflects on the matter will realize that the difficulties of establishing such bases on the shores of the St. Lawrence are so great as to render such a proceeding very unlikely. I have said in this house, and I have said it several times elsewhere, that the fuel capacity of modem submarines is ample to allow them to cruise from their bases in Europe to the shores of the north American continent, to do their work there for some weeks even, and then to return to their base in Europe without the necessity of refuelling. A round trip from a submarine base at Lorient, for example, on the coast of Europe, to the St. Lawrence, is no more than six thousand miles. German submarines can cruise twice that distance, and some of them do even better than that. They can remain away from their base for many weeks. It is possible that refuelling is done from mother ships, as they are called1, somewhere on the sea, although we have no definite evidence of that.
I should like to point out that there have been many more sinkings in the gulf of Mexico area than in the St. Lawrence area. These two areas are comparable in that they are both bodies of water to which access can be obtained only through comparatively narrow straits and they are both protected by islands and peninsulas. Yet the gulf of Mexico, some two thousand miles further away from the European bases of German submarines than is the gulf of St. Lawrence, has had twice as many sinkings as the gulf of St. Lawrence has had, and I have heard nobody in the United States suggest that the whole United States fleet should be diverted1 from its other duties to protect the gulf of Mexico.
Some reference was made in the same debate to spies and to the fact that there might be some spies on the shores of the St. Lawrence.
I think that hon. members of this house, and I should hope hon. members of any house, would realize that it is very dangerous to begin to talk about spies at such a time as this. To publish information about spies or about the capture or the presence of spies, would be helpful to the enemy rather than helpful to this country.
I should like to say finally that in about two months time a new navigation season will open in the gulf and river St. Lawrence, and no one can prophesy what action will take place in that area during the navigation season. I believe I am safe in saying that every possible precaution will be taken by the Canadian armed services, the navy, the army and the air service, to deal with every situation which can be expected1 to develop. To cope adequately with a problem of this kind, however, involves the cooperation of citizens in the area and the cooperation of members of this house and of provincial legislatures. To disclose information which might be helpful to the enemy by asking questions in public or by making statements in public is not doing a service to this country. For the welfare of the parts of the country which are directly affected by this discussion, and for the protection of the lives of the men who must fight every threat which is made, I ask for all the cooperation that it is possible for hon. members of this house and for all the citizens of Canada to give to the armed services.

speechtext: When the house adjourned last night I was dealing with the problem which had arisen in western Canada in connection with the production of flax. speechtext:
Well, I could give the
minister the exact words, but in effect what he said was that so far as they could tell at the present time there were no indications that the flax acreage was to be increased this year as compared with last year, which is exactly the same thing. Subsequently statements were made by responsible officials of some of the departments that the flax acreage was to be increased. All I have to say, Mr. Speaker, is that this matter should be cleared up as quickly as possible in order that the confusion which has been caused to the farmers may be removed.
The Budget-Mr. Bence

Before I leave this subject. I might say just a word in connection with the processing of flax in this country. It appears that Canada produces considerably more flax for oil purposes than we can process. This information was given to the house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) on February 22, when he stated that the net marketable crop last year was 13,230,000 bushels, whereas the total capacity for flax processing in this country was only 6,395,000 bushels; and of course it may be that the explanation for the change in the policy of the administration with respect to this year's flax production is that we have not the flax processing plants on the north American continent. But, Mr. Speaker, in reply to the same question to which I referred a moment ago the information was given to this house that there were in operation, in Canada nine flax processing plants with one under construction. Three are in the city of Montreal; two are in the city of Toronto; one is at Baden; one is at Winnipeg; one is at St. Boniface; one is at Medicine Hat, and there is one under construction at Hamilton. What I should like to know, and what I believe many people in this country would like to know, is why a plant is being constructed in Hamilton, which is already surfeited with industries, where already they are having great difficulties in regard to housing and other matters, and where it will be many hundreds of miles from the source of supply. As I demonstrated last evening, the great bulk of the flax produced in this country for oil purposes is grown in Saskatchewan, which is the province more particularly interested in this problem than any other. But that province has no flax processing plant. I do not know the reason for this, but it does seem to me that if we are to have an effective and efficient war effort the government must have its mind continually trained on problems such as these. Here is the situation. We produce the flax in Saskatchewan, and we ship it to Hamilton or Toronto or Montreal or some other place in order to have it processed. If it were processed in Saskatchewan we would save a great deal of labour on the part of the employees of the railways; we would be able to use the freight cars for other purposes-

speechtext:
I did not say that. I sug
gested that if we were to have an efficient and economic war effort the government must train its mind1 on the problem of having these plants where they will be most effective; and surely if we are to solve some of the labour and transportation problems we now have on our hands the government should decide where these plants should be located in order most economically to produce these very necessary materials. Would it not have been far better to locate this new plant in the province of Saskatchewan, rather than in Hamilton, in order to avoid all these transportation difficulties? I dp not know how it came about that the plant was located in Hamilton, but what has the government done about it? What attempt has been made to solve these problems? To me this is a demonstration of a waste of man-power and effort which we cannot afford to have at this time, to which I shall refer more particularly in a moment.
I do not propose to deal specifically with anything set out in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, except to make some brief reference to the pay-as-you-earn plan. The whole question of the budget and all its ramifications was admirably covered in the speech delivered by the hon. member for Danfortb (Mr. Harris), and it gives me a great deal of pleasure indeed to congratulate the hon. member upon the diligence with which he prepared that address and the manner in which he delivered it in this house. In reference to the pay-as-you-earn plan I merely wish to emphasize that it is not the Ruml plan. As I see it, the difference between the Ruml plan and1 the plan which has been introduced by the Minister of Finance is that under the Ruml plan we would skip one year's taxes, while the minister's plan merely provides that we must pay two and a half year's taxes in the space of two years. The mistake the administration has made lies in the fact that last year they put into effect what I would refer to as a half-baked sort of Ruml plan, whereas if they had adopted the principle in toto last year we would have it on a proper basis this year. In my judgment the Ruml plan appealed to the people of Canada, but I rather fear that they will be disappointed in the plan that has been presented by the minister because, as I said before, in effect what it means is that over a period of two years we are to pay two and a half year's taxes.
During .the current year we shall be required to raise the sum. of $5,500,000,000, and whatever anyone else may say about it, I believe this is going to be a tremendous financial

The Budget-Mr. Bence
burden, particularly upon the small people of this country. Further drastic restrictions will have to be imposed, which will bring about a further lowering of our standard of living and in some cases, particularly in connection with those having small and rigid incomes, there will be a certain amount of want and suffering. And, Mr. Speaker, because the people of Canada are so vitally affected by the budget; because their standard of living is being reduced so drastically; furthermore and particularly because their loved ones and their friends are offering their lives in all parts of the world in defence of freedom, they are determined that the war effort of this country, from a production point of view, must be as efficient and as economical as it is humanly possible to make it. I do not desire to make any charges or to suggest that anything is wrong in the sense that there has been corruption, but in my opinion there has been a great deal of wastage in our war effort due to a lack of foresight and a lack of planning on the part of the administration. The flax situation, to which I referred a short while ago, is one small example of lack of foresight and planning so far as saving man-power, energy and material is concerned. As I see the picture there has been a lack of cohesion, a lack of coordination and a lack of long-range planning in connection with many phases of Canada's war effort. The position is this, that in many cases things have been done the hard way, and when they have been done the hard way they have been done the costly way. Many problems have not been squarely faced until they have been right upon us, and the methods then adopted to cope with them necessarily have been hastily conceived and badly carried out.
I have in mind at the present time one striking example, namely, the construction of temporary buildings in Ottawa for the purpose of endeavouring to house practically the whole of our administrative effort in this beautiful city. I referred to this before when I spoke in the debate in reply to the speech from the throne, and I intend to refer to it again, because it is the kind of suggestion which hon. members should make to the government in order to relieve some of the unnecessary wastage that is going on.
First of all I would point out that there seems to be an attitude of mind that it is necessary for every part of the administration to be housed in Ottawa, and the person who is in control of any administrative effort seems to feel he must be down here at what he considers the head of affairs. If the situation is considered carefully, and if these people would only look at the whole picture, they
would realize that they can carry on their work just as easily in some other part of the country, and if they did there would be no necessity for the erection of these temporaiy buildings at tremendous cost.
In a return to the house on June 1 last it was shown that since the beginning of the war there had been constructed or there were then under construction in Ottawa eleven temporary buildings and one annex, at a total cost of $5,411,099.76. On the first of June of last year only half of those buildings had been built; the rest of them were still under construction. This was the condition, mark you, practically three years after the beginning of the war, when labour and materials were getting scarce; yet half of the buildings were being constructed at that time. That might have been all right at the beginning of the war, when we had plenty of labour available and an abundance of materials; but every possible step should have been taken to avoid that unnecessary expenditure and that unnecessary condition at a time when the material was so badly needed for other purposes.
Not only that, but the condition is continuing. On March 8 there were tabled the answers to some questions I had asked earlier. One question was as to how many more temporary buildings were to be erected in Ottawa, and at what cost. I received the answer, with respect to the Royal Canadian Air Force, that land and buildings for certain constructions were to cost $312,000. Land and buildings for another department were to cost $54,205; and in addition to that, for the purpose of office accommodation for the wartime prices and trade board, there was to be a building costing $450,000.
At the same time may I point out that there appeared in the press of February 26 the statement that the government approved the building programme under the National Housing Act, and that in Ottawa and vicinity a million dollars was to be spent on the construction of houses. Of that amount a quarter of a million dollars was to be paid by the government.'
I suggest that in large measure the reason for this lies in the fact that there has been such over-congestion in Ottawa, and so much of the work has been done here that it is necessary to go on putting more nails, more steel, more lumber and more energy into coping with problems which have been created by the government's action. We need that labour, we need that lumber, we need that steel and those nails for other purposes, and I suggest to the house that there should be no
The Budget;-Mr. Bence

building in Canada to-day which is not absolutely required for our war effort. I say that because I believe we have sufficient buildings in this country to take care of our war programme, and we must make the most of what we have. We need this labour to make munitions of war, to produce foodstuffs, and for dozens of other essential things. We need, indeed, the labour and the lumber for the preservation of our own people.
The other day we received an announcement through the mail, one which had been given out by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) indicating that the wood fuel situation in Canada is desperate. It showed that next year there was likely to be a worse condition, because not only are we using up last year's supply, but that lumber which was being cut and was intended for next year is already being used in order to heat houses and to do necessary cooking. We know, too, that there has been a desperate shortage of coal this winter, and that that shortage will be even greater next winter.
If this extra labour is available it should be used to produce what is necessary to keep our people from freezing. The labour should be directed to other purposes than erecting more buildings in Ottawa. If the situation had been properly canvassed many of those buildings would not have been necessary. In Canada to-day many buildings are being used for non-essential purposes. Many factories are still producing non-essential goods. Why was not the whole situation canvassed thoroughly by someone with over-all authority who could say to these various departments: That building is not necessary, because we can send you here, or we can send you there? Why is there not someone who would have the job of investigating and determining whether or not certain factories could be used for these purposes, if at the present time they are not producing something essential?
The buildings being erected in Ottawa are temporary, and they are intended as nothing else. Many stores are curtailing their hours of sale because of lack of goods to sell and lack of labour. Several examples can be found right here in Ottawa. Along some of the main streets one can see cards in the store windows stating they will not be open until such-and-such an hour. Why can we not work out a plan under which some of these store buildings could be used for housing administrative workers? Why could not stores be doubled up? There is no necessity for having two stores open a half day when one could be open a whole day and the other be made available for other purposes.

Large department stores find that their counters are bare because they have not the goods to sell. I am not criticizing anyone because the goods are not there. We cannot continue to produce non-essential consumer goods. This is a necessary result of our war programme. There is no reason why all these stores should be operating when one building could do the work now being done by four or five. Some of them could then be used for the purposes for which the temporary buildings are being constructed. I do not think this is an unreasonable suggestion. It may be the kind of thing which would be considered drastic in peace time; but when we are in a life and death struggle we can put up with inconveniences. We shall have to put up with many more before we have finished.
There are many possibilities which could be canvassed with a view to providing necessary office accommodation. Let us go outside of Ottawa, to the various cities across Canada, and utilize the buildings that are available. But even in Ottawa I think more diligence could have been shown in finding available accommodation.
I believe members of parliament could be asked to put themselves to some small inconvenience. In many cases we have comfortable private offices. Many of them are now accommodating only one member. Surely we could make some kind of arrangement to double up-and I am sure the senators would agree to a similar arrangement. They would probably agree to come from the other side of the building, and we could make some provision whereby we could provide accommodation for some of the additional workers now in Ottawa.
Every possible step should be taken to avoid unnecessary construction at the present time. This is not a question of money; it is a question of man-power and material. If there is already office space in the country which can be used, then certainly we should not be constructing new buildings in Ottawa.
A moment ago I referred to the fuel problem, and I shall conclude my remarks by making a further reference to it. As I stated, the Minister of Munitions and Supply issued a press release from his department in which it was asserted that the wood fuel situation was serious, and he made certain suggestions as to how the problem might be solved. One was that the government was going to pay an additional dollar per cord to the fuel dealers. Another was that farmers might go to work cutting fuel in their off season, and that they would not thereby lose the privileges they have at the present time under the national selective service regulations. I

The Budget-Mr. MacKenzie (Lambton)
presume that some legislation is to be introduced or some order in council passed to make that official. At present it is merely a statement that the selective service officers will consider farmers doing this work as not losing their exemption under the regulations. But I do not know how that is to be accomplished officially. In any event the problem will not be solved in that way, because the farmers are just getting ready to put in their crops, and this wood fuel problem is one that must be solved now. Next winter will be too late. The fuel problem is a very serious one, and the people will suffer unnecessary hardships if it is not tackled immediately, and with courage, and with some measure of efficiency and effectiveness. The problem is of first importance and its solution is the job of those who have been given a mandate to carry on the affairs of this country. The only solution as I see it is a proper plan of allocation of labour which will take out of unnecessary production workers who can be put at this particular kind of labour. We have not yet effectively tackled this question of taking workers out of non-essential work. But when we face the danger of our people suffering and even freezing to death next winter, something should be done without further delay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to discuss the budget I first want to pay tribute to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) for bringing down the budget so early in the session. It must have meant long and arduous hours of labour to bring down a budget providing for the raising of such a colossal sum of money. It is very difficult indeed to allocate the burden of taxation fairly among the taxpayers of Canada when taxation is called for upon such a stupendous scale, but I believe that the people as a whole regard this budget as a very good one and are prepared to accept the challenge to work and save which the Minister of Finance made to the people in his closing remarks the other night.
I wish to discuss particularly some problems pertaining to agriculture. A return that was brought down the other day was interesting to me. It showed that in the fiscal year 1942-43 only about 1,500 farmers paid income tax to an amount of approximately $150,000. The minister's estimate of income tax receipts for the fiscal year 1942-43, which ends on March 31, 1943, was approximately $842,000,000. That means that the farmers paid approximately five cents each in income tax, because according to the census of 1941 the farm population comprises 28 per cent of the total
population of the country, or about three million people. If this is a fair estimate of what the farmers are supposed to pay in income tax, they are not getting a fair share of the national income. If we are ever to settle the problems of agriculture satisfactorily the remuneration for the products of the farm must be raised to a comparable basis with the products of industry. We must also provide some relief from the drudgery of farm work, and make farm homes more attractive, with conveniences more in line with those found in the homes of city dwellers. We are asked to produce, but the farmers get very little encouragement to produce. It is true that in most long wars food products play an important part in the long run, and that is true of this war. It is probable that the foodstuffs of the world will play an important part in the final outcome of this war. That is why our farmers are being asked to produce more of all kinds of farm products.
In the matter of hydro extension, the farmers, and I am speaking particularly of Ontario, have been discriminated against. About two years ago an order was issued that no new installations of hydro should be made in rural communities. Three factors entered into this picture. There was the hydroelectric power commission, the power controller and the metals controller. The order provided that no new installation of hydro could be made, except under permit, if the home was more than 250 feet away from the transmission line. During this time houses were being built in towns, cities and incorporated villages and hydro was installed there without any restrictions at all. Fixtures also were allowed to be installed. But all this was denied to the rural people. In many of the rural districts the hydro transmission lines run down the concession lines, but the farmers were denied the privilege of hydro. At the same time this right was extended to city dwellers. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of rural Ontario are more entitled to the use of hydro power than people who live in incorporated villages, cities and towns, because our farmers have to work long hours before daylight and after dark and have great need of hydro power. I am glad to note that the hydro commission is now cooperating with the controllers on a scheme whereby hydro can be extended to the rural people. Less than thirty per cent of the people in rural Ontario have hydro or running water in their homes, and until we can make these conveniences available to people in the rural districts we can never solve the problem of a happy and contented rural population. I
1138	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. MacKenzie (Lambton)
shall discuss agricultural problems further, probably on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. But for the moment I wish to talk about economies on parliament hill, in the houses of parliament as now constituted.
The question has been raised in this chamber by hon. members of practically all groups, by the press throughout Canada, and by individuals in public speeches and addresses, that the cost of government services is too high. Even prior to the present war the matter was one of public discussion. To go back a few years, around 1906 to 1908, the expenditure at Ottawa was approximately forty to forty-five million dollars. In 1939, the budget which was approved before the outbreak of war, and which made provision for a large expansion of national defence, was about $550,000,000. The provision for expansion of the Department of National Defence was made because war seemed inevitable, although some groups in this house did not appear to think so. Many hon. members will recall when old age pensions were first discussed in this house, and also pensions for the blind. Everybody admitted that there was merit in those demands, particularly those on behalf of people who were so unfortunate as to be blind, but the invariable answer from the government of the day, from the then Minister of Finance and his colleagues on the treasury benches was, "We appreciate all that, but where will you get the money from?" We are now in the fourth year of the war, and war, at best, is waste, not only of material things but of life itself, and that of our own soldiers as well. The peoples of Europe, Africa and Asia are sacrificing their lives by thousands if not millions. In the fourth year of the war we are budgeting for an expenditure of five and a half billion dollars, or practically ten times as much as we budgeted for in 1939. Therefore it is pretty hard for the people to go back to the belief that if the occasion demands, whether it be a national crisis or a specifically economic crisis, the money cannot be procured if it has to be got. But the people would feel more satisfied if they were assured that money was being carefully expended and rigid economy practised with respect to government expenditures. We should turn from habits of extravagance to habits of saving. As it is, the fear is expressed by many people throughout the country, particularly where large construction work goes on, that the money is not being carefully expended, that rigid economy is not being practised, and that the country's savings are being wasted. We are asked to save; we are even forced to save. We are expected to refrain from luxuries and to be content with the necessities of life.

I do not intend to enter into a general discussion of whether Canada is overgoverned. If I did, I think the answer would be emphatically, yes. In this dominion, with approximately eleven and a half million people, there are over four thousand money-spending municipalities. Apart from that, in this dominion and nine provinces there are over eight hundred and fifty lawmakers-more than in any other country in the world with the possible exceptions of the United States and Great Britain. It is true that Ontario, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia have made moves to lessen the number of their legislators, and we here could very well follow their example. Following the 1931 census, provision was made for two hundred and forty-five members of the House of Commons. In accordance with the census of 1941 the number will be reduced, particularly from Saskatchewan and Manitoba, but there could very well be a further reduction by a general reallocation of seats throughout the dominion. I do not propose to discuss at any length the position of the upper chamber, because it was a subject of debate at some length both last year and this year. In fairness it must be recognized,
I	believe, that the upper chamber is composed of honourable and capable men. But if we go back we shall find that in 1891 the Liberal platform contained a plank called "senate reform". The subject was debated in this chamber at some length in 1909 and 1910, and at that time the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen voted for senate reform. Since that time he has been in the upper house and out of it, but there is no record that he made any reference to it while he was there. It was, I believe, in 1942 that the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Gladstone), speaking in this house on July 7, said, as reported at page 3991 of
II	ansard:
The other house should be used or disbanded altogether. There are highly qualified and experienced men in that house who should be given an opportunity to render service to Canada. We are paying them and letting them die of dry rot.
This House of Commons was in session for six months last year, and during that time the upper house met only twice for short periods. It is true that just recently, when the 1942 war appropriation supplementary estimates of around $858,000,000 were passed in this house, there were at that time, according to the press, only twenty members of the upper house who thought it important enough to assemble to discuss that matter of a mere $858,000,000.
Again, we find that last year, as reported in Hansard of May 6, at page 2183, the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) said:

The Budget-
-Mr. MacKenzie (Lambton)
Mr. Speaker, in view of the urgency of the situation and the desirablity of strengthening in every possible way our parliamentary institutions by recruiting thereto men and women of outstanding ability, will the Prime Minister tell the house when he will be in a position to announce the appointment of men and women of ability to the Senate of Canada to fill the many vacancies at present existing?
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) replied:
I shall be glad to take note of my hon. friend's desire to be considered in that connection.
Why should such appointments be necessary? If we have any thought of reducing government costs in this country and in the House of Commons, should they not be reduced in the other chamber as well? Either the number of members should be reduced or that house should be abolished altogether. As the hon. member for Wellington South said last year, they should be given some useful work. Why can they not institute some useful work of their own? I notice that this year they are appointing some committees to study rehabilitation and reestablishment, and also social security. That is fine, but I believe they should also be able to do something useful to help the House of Commons in the problems which annually confront us in this chamber. For instance, a war expenditures committee appointed by this house has been operating for the last two years. It is composed of twenty-four members. They have done some useful work. A question was asked in the house recently about the cost of that committee. I am not in a position to say how much it is, but it must be considerable. The members of the committee get $15 a day, and there are additional expenses in connection with stenographers, stationery, and so forth. Is there any reason in the world why the upper house should not perform the duties of that war expenditures committee?

That is what is provided. Whether they take it or not, I do not know. For several years we have been talking in this house about appointing a committee to study the estimates, but nothing has been done. Every session since I have been here the Ottawa Journal or the Ottawa Citizen has commented on the millions that are passed in a minute or two in the closing days of the session. Is there any reason why the upper house should not study these estimates, so that
when they come here for final adoption we shall be able to vote on them at least intelligently? It is true there is an opposition, and it is rather amusing to watch them at times feebly asking questions about this or that expenditure. The information given is supplied by the departments, and those asking the questions get very little information.
These estimates are prepared by the different departments. In reality most business is done by orders in council and the estimates are prepared by the civil service. In my opinion the upper chamber is not given any useful or contributory work to do. On different occasions the Prime Minister has stated that he favoured senate reform. In view of the fact that there are eleven vacancies, I suggest that he pull the plug and let them all go. It would mean a saving of at least $380,000 a year, besides saving other expenses.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: This house cannot abolish the senate.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
True, we cannot abolish the senate, but if we refrain from appointing them it will abolish itself in time. Last year the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. McLean) said, something about government costs. I am quite in accord with what he said. If we are asking the people of this country to save and conserve, to exercise economy, I think we should set our own house in order and practise economy here, thereby giving an example to the Canadian public. Speaking in the house last year, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said;
In my judgment, parliament is more and more on trial at the bar of public opinion. There is something wrong with this House of Commons. I am not reflecting on the house and I do not know what is the cause, but there is something wrong with it and I have asked myself, "is it the fault of the government in any way?"
Let me offer some suggestions which I think will help to solve some of the problems that confronted the Minister of Finance when he asked that question. I believe, and I think many other hon. members agree, that far too much of the time of the house is taken up in asking questions of the members of the government who sit on the front benches. Much of the information asked for in these questions could be obtained from the departments without taking up the time of the house. I quite appreciate that some questions have to do with matters of national urgency, but there are many others that should be directed to the departments.
Many of the speeches made in this house are made for home consumption, for the pur-

The Budget-Mr. MacKenzie (Lambton)
pose of getting them on Hansard. On February 25, 1892, an order in council was passed regulating the franking privileges enjoyed by hon. members of this house and of the senate, as governed by section 43 of the Post Office Act. This section reads as follows:
Letters and other mailable matter addressed to or sent by the Speaker or Clerk of the Senate or of the House of Commons at the seat of government shall be free of Canada postage, and letters and other mailable matter addressed to or by any member of either house at the seat of government during any session of parliament, or to any of the members at the seat of government as aforesaid, during the ten days next before the meeting of parliament, shall be free of Canada postage.
These franking privileges have been abused from time to time by the members of this house and the members of the other house. Reports have come to the Post Office Department-this is definitely on record-to the effect that members have abused this franking privilege by conducting their private business under the frank. It is also true that members and senators living outside Ottawa have sent mail in bulk to the Speaker of the House of Commons or the Speaker of the Senate respectively to be mailed under the frank.
The reading of speeches is still adhered to. The rule should be either that we should be permitted to read them or that we should not be permitted to read them. When some hon. members make speeches-the house knows this is. correct-they have thousands of copies printed which are mailed free on government stationery to their constituents.
Mr. MaeNICOL: The hon. member knows that we have to pay for the printing of those speeches.

I will come to that a little later. Some members or groups of members in this house use the House of Commons and the Post Office De-

partment as a clearing-house through which to spread their political propaganda and doctrines to their constituents at the public expense. There is no doubt about that. I am not saying what particular members they were. I have seen trucks loaded with this stationery to such an extent that one would think they were moving the stationery department. These trucks are filled up with literature being sent to the paste room to be mailed at the taxpayers' expense. The stationery supplied to the members of the House of Commons during the last few years has cost from $35,000 to $40,000 a year. According to a report which I received, 400,000 Hansard envelopes were supplied to members of the House of Commons in 1942. Surely the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) does not contend that he is paying for these Hansard envelopes.
Mr. MaeNICOL: I said that I paid for the printing of any speech that I mail out.

And the Hansard envelopes?

speechtext:
If this franking privilege granted to the members of the House of Commons and the Senate were abolished, it would reduce the length of the session by months and the stenographic and messenger staffs could be reduced by one-third. It would save tens of thousands of dollars of the taxpayers' money. Imagine the cost of transporting all this mail that goes out free!
I feel sorry for the rural mail carriers who have to deliver this mail up and down the country because it is all sent out free of postage.

The Budget-Mr. MacKenzie (Lambton)
Then there is another factor that we must remember. A man might want to start a leadership league, and he would advertise in all the papers and send them free to members of the House of Commons. The house will remember that two years ago hundreds and thousands of letters came to this house because they were free of postage. If the two post offices in the houses of parliament were amalgamated there would be a great saving. At the present time there are two post offices, under the jurisdiction of the respective Speakers. They should be amalgamated and placed under the direction of the Postmaster General. It is claimed by the post office authorities that the franking of mail matter of the Senate and the House of Commons each year would amount to approximately $55,000 or $60,000 if postage were paid. I admit that in the original plan the intention of the franking privilege was that members of the House of Commons should be able to conduct their correspondence relating to government work free of postage. And in view of the income tax that hon. members have to pay, it probably would be a hardship to abolish that privilege. They should be allowed a small amount for postage on their mail while parliament is in session. The present legislation regarding franking was enacted many years ago, and it applies to the other government departments as well. It reads as follows:
All letters and other mailable matter addressed to or sent by the governor general, or sent to or by any department of tlie government at the seat of government, shall be free of Canada postage under such regulations as are, from time to time, made in that respect by governor in council.
Post office officials to whom I have talked at different times regarding this are of opinion that the abolition of the franking privilege of the House of Commons and the Senate would do more for economy and save more than any other single factor. To be sure, if none of the departments were free from postage it would probably mean taking money out of one pocket to put it in the other, but it would more than any other factor induce them to conserve and save. A few years ago the cost of mail sent out from the departments was approximately $750,000. That has increased to $2,500,000 and is increasing daily. So that if this franking privilege were abolished it would help more than any other factor to solve the problem of extravagance at Ottawa.
If freedom of speech is the bulwark of democracy, let us not talk it to death in this house. It is true that in the United States congress the members may send their speeches
to the Speaker and have them printed in the record without the trouble of delivering or reading them in congress.

speechtext:
Also if he wishes to have it taken as read he can hand it in. I am confident that seventy-five per cent of the speeches made in this house are not listened to at all except by the Hansard reporters.
Can one imagine why we should have two post offices in this building, manned by two separate staffs, one under the jurisdiction of the Speaker of the Senate, and the other under the jurisdiction of the House of Commons? If we do not change our rules regarding these houses of parliament, a wave of sentiment throughout the country will change our rales for us. I think that of all systems of government, ours, which is copied from the British parliamentary system, is the very worst. It was invented two hundred and fifty years ago to break the power of a parliament which was not disposed to do anything but compete for places on the treasury benches and raise money for war against Louis XIV.
I shall offer a few suggestions to the Minister of Finance and to this government which I think would go a long way to solve the question of what is wrong with our houses of parliament here in Ottawa.
The first is the amalgamation of the post offices in the parliament buildings into one and to place that one entirely under the jurisdiction of the Postmaster General. The second is the abolition of the free franking privilege of members of the House of Commons and the Senate as well as of all government departments. The third is the abolition of the senate or at least the reform of it. Members of the senate should retire at least at retiring age.

Then I say that public sentiment believes that at least there should be a retiring age for the members of the senate, because every other public body has a retiring age. And fourth, I would say that there should be a change in the rules of this house so as to provide that private members must confine their speeches to twenty minutes instead of forty as is now the situation.
I am sorry if I have transgressed the rules, but I make these statements because I believe that we are abusing the privileges and rights that belong to us as a parliament.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am rather amused at the remarks of the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie) who has just taken his seat. He went out of his way to reprimand other hon. members for speaking in such manner as would tend to give them publicity in their own constituency; yet I would think the speech of the hon. member would be a proper one to have been made in a Liberal caucus. That is where he should have his fights; after all, a Liberal government is in power and it is up to them to take measures to counteract the things of which the hon. member is complaining. Further, I wish to say that the members of our group never do speak for home consumption; they try to give something constructive.
It would appear from the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) that farmers are to receive no increase in income despite the universally recognized fact that all costs of agricultural production have gone up. It must be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that agriculture is this nation's basic industry and that without a prosperous and virile agricultural population this country will never reach the height of prosperity that is so essential to the welfare of Canadians and so necessary to our war effort. Agriculture is also a vital war industry, just as truly as are those other industries which are producing the munitions of war, and I believe that unless we recognize that fact and face the problems of agriculture immediately, there is grave danger of an economic collapse on our food
I Mr. Speaker.]
front. That is why I wish to direct my remarks this afternoon more particularly to agricultural matters, because in my opinion such a collapse on the agricultural front would be just as disastrous as a collapse in the manufacture of the munitions of war.
Such direction as the government has given agriculture so far has, in my opinion, resulted only in confusion, not only among the farmers but among the ministers of the crown themselves; and on account of this lack of proper direction the farmers are becoming desperate, for they see no solution of the problems with which they are faced. I think it is a well known fact that many leaders in agriculture are now coming to the point where they are implying, if not suggesting, that the only way in which agriculture can bring its problems definitely to the attention of the government is by going on a sitdown strike. That is not the best solution, yet for some reason or another it seems to be the only way in which not only agriculture but-industry itself, and especially organized labour, can get results, either by the threat of a strike or by actually striking. That may not be the best thing to do, but I do not see how else the government is to be moved. That is not a healthy condition to have in this country.
One of the matters in which I am particularly interested is the problem of man-power. With this in mind I have gone over the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as well as the budget speech of the Minister of Finance to try to find out what is the proposed man-power policy in regard to agriculture. I must confess that it is very confusing to me, as I am sure it must be equally confusing to the farmers of western Canada and, in fact, to the farmers throughout Canada as a whole. I am amazed at the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture toward the manpower problem. I think it is safe and fair to say that he does not fear the man-power problem at all, in fact that he sees no shortage of man-power on our farms. He is peculiar in that regard; certainly he is the only western man I know of who does not see that difficulty looming before us. On February 9 the minister made a speech dealing with this problem, and in the course of his remarks he referred to the large number of farmers and farmers' sons and daughters who had left the land and gone into other occupations, particularly in war industries. I wish to quote a few of his words, as they appear at page 269 of Hansard: Although we did that, what has been the result? Not long ago I was speaking in Saskatoon to a group of farmers. I had been asked the question that has been asked in the house on numerous occasions since this debate began: Is there going to be a labour shortage

The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
this year? I had to say that we had been building up our objectives year after year while the number of persons on the farms has been going down year by year; we have not yet reached the peak of production under these conditions, and until we have done so I cannot say with absolute assurance that lack of labour will prevent us from reaching our objectives this year.
I do not think I can be accused of being unfair when I say that the minister does not view the labour problem with alarm, for he says he is quite sure we shall reach our objectives this year without any additional farm help. He goes on to say:
I have this to say as well, and every member of this house, on both sides of the house, knows it is a fact. For eight years before this war started, boys and girls brought up on farms never intended to remain on the farm. They had been directed, from their childhood up, towards some other activity, but they found it impossible to get off the farm.
It is probably quite true that large numbers of people, particularly young people, were extremely anxious to leave the farms, but why? I think the answer should be obvious to the minister or to anyone. The reason was that there was not a decent living to be had on the farm for the farmer and his whole family. Agricultural conditions were such that they could not maintain a decent standard of living, and consequently they sought employment elsewhere. Then he goes on to say:
With regard to overall production, our farms to-day, with these 250,000 gone, are producing more than they ever produced before.
He is again emphasizing the fact that there is no danger from a man-power shortage, and he is so emphatic in that regard that he concludes his remarks with these words:
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that those of us who have been speaking on agriculture have been emphasizing the necessity for labour during the coming year. I am oing to repeat that I have not been convinced y any arguments I have heard in the house, nor am I convinced by our experiences of the past, that we cannot reach the objectives which we have placed before the farmers of this country for this fourth year of war.
With that summary he definitely concludes his argument, saying that although we have asked for a much greater production from the farms in this, the fourth year of war, he sees no difficulty whatever in reaching that objective with the present labour on the farms, despite the fact that more than 250,000 people have left the land. But the Minister of Agriculture seems to have overlooked the fact that the only ones now left on the farm, as a result of government policy, are the more elderly people. All the young men have been conscripted for the army, and the young women have joined the armed forces as well.
In some instances, of course, they have gone to industries. The result is that the only ones left are those people who are no longer young, who are not mechanically minded and who have never had any experience in operating tractors or combines. These are the developments in agriculture, and as a result farmers will face difficulties this year.
The Minister of Agriculture may say that we do not want our people to raise too much grain, and that he would like them to devote their time and energy to stock-raising. But if he takes that view I think he is definitely showing his ignorance in regard to farming because, without question, there is a great deal more work, especially in the winter time, when a farmer has to feed and water stock, whether it be cattle or hogs. If farmers are to increase their cattle and hog production, then they will have a great deal more labour than ever before was required on their farms. It seems strange that the minister does not realize that in the west to-day the farmers face a peculiar situation. I believe I am conservative when I say that at least forty-five per cent of crops are still out, and unthreshed. The reason why the grain is still out is that, through government policy, the young men have been taken off the farms. Last fall, when threshing operations were in progress, there were not sufficient young men to make full crews on threshing machines. The result was that the rate of threshing was greatly reduced. With the early fall-and I am not blaming the government for that-over forty-five per cent of the crop was left to lie under the snow.
But the minister disregards that entirely. He says quite definitely the farmers do not need to worry about help on their farms, because they have sufficient help now. That is his statement, despite the fact that over 250,000 have been taken off the farms. That is one point of view.
I said a moment ago that there has been confusion in the government itself, among cabinet ministers, in regard to the man-power problem. I should like to prove that assertion, and I believe I can do it to the satisfaction of the house. I have set out the view of the Minister of Agriculture in regard to this problem. Now for a few moments I shall refer to what the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has had to say. As I read the minister's statements in regard to man-power I believe the remarks made by the last speaker were appropriate when he said that much of this stuff was just for purposes of propaganda. I believe the proposals of the Minister of Labour were mostly that.
1144	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
Hon. members will recall that whea the minister spoke on February 26, as reported at page 741 of Hansard, he referred to his concern about the question of man-power, and read a special letter on this subject from Mr. MacNamara which had been sent out to the boards. The minister was turning his attention here, there and everywhere in an endeavour to find men for the farms. Why? Why was the Minister of Labour so anxious to get men for the farms this summer when the minister in charge of agriculture-the Minister of Agriculture himself-says there is no danger whatsoever? It would appear that the Minister of Labour has not consulted the Minister of Agriculture in this regard-either that or he is woefully ignorant of the facts.

speechtext: I do not think a statement like that is very elevating, when the hon. member does not even know what he is talking about.

I think the Minister of Labour will agree with me that the Minister of Agriculture does not view with the least bit of alarm the man-power problem on the farms. I do not hear the minister make any remark on the point, and accordingly I take his silence as consent.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will put the facts on Hansard, and hon. members can judge for themselves. I do not think anyone will doubt what I said with regard to the stand taken by the Minister of Agriculture.
Now then, let us see what the Minister of Labour had to say in regard to the regulations concerning man-power. I have said he was looking here, there and everywhere else; and I am convinced it was mostly propaganda stuff. I say that because this is his solution: He is going to take boys and girls from the schools, and put them on the farms. Why put boys and girls from the schools on the farms if they are not needed? Anyone who has worked on a farm knows it is not a summer

resort. We tried that plan out to a degree
last year, and it was- successful only to a certain extent. But those of us from the west know that the young people who went from eastern Canada to work on the western farms, despite their willingness-and I am not questioning that for a moment-just did not know how to go about their work. If the Minister of Labour thinks for a minute that these young and inexperienced people, some of whom never saw a cow in their lives, and the great majority of whom did not know how to run a combine or how to work efficiently, were sufficient to answer the need, then I say he is mistaken. Some of them did not know how to handle a fork. True, they were earnest, and some worked almost to the point of exhaustion; but even then they did not accomplish much.
Despite their work, over 45 per cent of the crop is now under the snow. I believe I have given sufficient proof that that policy will not work; and yet that is where the Minister of Labour is to get his help for the farms. If that does not work, what will he do? He will put prisoners of war and internees to work on the farms. I suggest that in doing so, he is just beating around the bush, and that he is not really serious in his attempt to solve the problem-if there is a problem, because the Minister of Agriculture says there is not.
It may be necessary to put some of those people on the farms, but I suggest that the Minister of Labour will have difficulty in doing it. There might not be the same danger from using prisoners of war on farms as there would be from using them in industrial plants. But certainly the element of danger is not eliminated. We know that a prisoner of war could just as effectively interfere with agricultural production as he could with production in industry. For instance, it would be very simple for one of them to ruin a tractor in ten minutes. He could destroy a combine and thereby impair the efficiency of agricultural production. There again I fear the Minister of Labour will have difficulties. Whether he believes seriously that either of the two procedures I have mentioned are sufficient to settle the man-power question, or that they will be effective, I cannot say. But from a practical point of view his suggestion does not appear sound to me.
If that does not work-and, you see, these are all so vague; all these propositions by the Minister of Labour are just straw men to take care of a problem the Minister of Agriculture says does not exist-the Minister of Labour will try something else. If that does not work he will draft the conscientious objectors. If that does not work he will take men from the

The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
reserve army who can establish that they are urgently needed on the farms. It is not up to the farmers, but up to the individuals themselves, to establish that they are urgently needed on the farms. These men whom he will take and put to work on the farms are men in the lower medical categories who have been rejected for the army on account of physical unfitness. In all seriousness I suggest to the Minister of Labour-I cannot believe that he has ever been on a farm-that a farm is no health resort, and if the farmers are to be compelled to take these men who are physically unfit the minister will find himself in difficulty again. I can speak from practical experience, and I wish to assure him that work on the farm requires a healthy body. It is exceedingly heavy work; the hours are very long. If a man is not in good physical condition he simply cannot stand up to the strain, and agricultural production will suffer in consequence.
I come now to the last suggestion, and it amuses me as I am sure it did the Minister of Labour himself when he put it down. His last suggestion is the temporary closing of manufacturing plants. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we have not reached the stage where we have to close down our production plants in order to take care of the man-power shortage on the farms. Does that indicate careful planning? Surely the Minister of Labour is not serious in his suggestion that our production plants must close down. If so, why? It is true that at Calgary two or three hundred men have been laid off work at the Ogden shops and it is likely that more men will be laid off there. But if we have to start to close down our production plants to take care of the labour shortage on the farm, then definitely there must be something wrong with our production planning. I cannot think that the Minister of Labour is serious in that suggestion. I have a clipping here from the Ottawa Journal of February 25, 1943, which, discussing the minister's emergency farm labour plan, says:
Most drastic feature of the farm labour programme was the plan for the calling up for agricultural service men now in low medical categories. It was believed that the men drafted for this work would draw army pay-not less than $45 per month and full maintenance-to be paid by the farmers employing them.
If that is true, and I do not hear the Minister of Labour contradicting it - the Minister of Labour can take this as a joke, but the farmers do not consider it a joke-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not taking it as a joke. It is my hon. friend.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do say that either the Minister of Labour or the
Minister of Agriculture cannot be serious about this man-power shortage on the farms when he would make this recommendation. He is going to make the farmer pay $45 a month, plus all maintenance charges, for men in low medical categories who take up farm work despite the fact that we cannot have any increased prices for agricultural products and despite the fact that the farmer is able to sell only so many bushels under the quota system. If that does not work, the minister will then see what he can do about sending the women out to work on the farms. If that does not show a sad state of confusion over this manpower shortage problem I should like to know what would. I suggest to the Minister of Labour and to the Minister of Agriculture that if they want to learn the best way to solve agricultural problems, let them consult the farmers themselves. Then they will get a solution. It is not sufficient for these two ministers to disregard the farmers as not knowing how to handle their own problems. When an industrial problem comes up you go to the industrialists, and properly so. I wonder what the business men, the industrialists who are producing war supplies, would say if the government went to them and said: If you want any more help, any green hands to train in your factory, you must bear all that expense alone-you must pay them so much per month, plus their maintenance. Why, they simply would not pay any attention to the Minister of Labour or the Minister of Agriculture or anybody else because that is not the way in 'which business is done. That is not the way in which business has been done since the beginning of this war. When we were training men for war industry, almost without exception every war contract was on a cost-plus basis; when green hands were sent into these war industries to be trained, that expense was added1 to the cost of producing the product, and the industries got their profit on top of those costs.
I should like to read a letter in regard to the difficulties of agriculture with respect to man-power. This letter comes to me from men who are right at the source of the trouble and know what they are talking about. It is from the Drumheller board of trade. These men are business men and farmers. They are right on the ground and know their own problems, and I would suggest that the Minister of Labour pay some heed to this. The letter is addressed to myself, and is dated, Drumheller, February 6, 1943. It reads:
Our board have written Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture), Hon. J. A. MacKinnon (Minister of Trade and Commerce) and Hon.
1146	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
Humphrey Mitchell (Minister of Labour), pointing out the serious situation in the big Drumheller agricultural district as regards the unharvested 1942 crop and seeking their cooperation in having sufficient men released from the Canadian forces to assist in taking off the balance of the 1942 crop as soon as it is possible to get at this work.
A survey of the situation would go to show that there is about 45 per cent of the 1942 crop in this district yet to be harvested, while some of the farmers were only able to harvest 10 per cent of their 1942 crop before the early winter set in and made further harvest work impossible.
Of course, so many farm workers enlisted or took war jobs, while the outstanding record of enlistments from this valley and the shortage of coal miners made it impossible to replace these men on the farms. Then, again, labour from outside was impossible to secure. Bad harvest weather and an extra early winter put the finishing touches on one of the most disappointing harvest seasons in our district's history.
However, you know the situation in Alberta and it is not necessary to elaborate further, but the main point is that the only solution, in our board's opinion, is to release a sufficient number of men from the Canadian forces to make possible the harvesting of the balance of the 1942 crop and that arrangements should be made right away so that when it is possible to do this work there will be no delay in dispatching the necessary men to the various points in the prairie provinces.
This work must be done before the regular spring work and if a plan is adopted now and the machinery created so that when the call goes out for men, then things will run smoothly.
Naturally, the problem is being considered at Ottawa at the present time-
They ought to know in what manner it is being considered.

but it must not be forgotten that there is a shortage of men on the farms right now and even if no more farmers or farm workers are called up the farmers will not be able to cope with the 1942 crop situation unless they get the assistance along the lines our board suggests. The unharvested 1942 crop is too vital to the nation not to be harvested in its entirety.
Thanking you in advance for your usual kind cooperation in this urgent and important matter, I am, upon behalf of our board,
Faithfully yours,
John A. Mackay,
Secretary.
These men realize the difficulty and are pointing it out to the government. Here we have one cabinet minister saying that there is no danger at all; that we shall produce this much larger crop than we have ever asked for before; that we shall reach the maximum of production for 1943, and that no more farm help is needed. But these men who are right on the ground know differently. The other day the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) outlined a questionnaire which was sent from the municipal district of Wainwright, in a different part of the country altogether, and they have the same

idea. I will not take time to put the questionnaire on Hansard, because the house is already informed of it.
I wish now to turn my attention for a while to parity prices, because I find just as much confusion in the government ranks over this matter as there is over the man-power problem-and goodness knows that is bad enough. Let us see what has happened in this country regarding agricultural prices since this Liberal government took office in 1935. I recall that when we came to this house in that year the price of wheat was S7J cents a bushel. But immediately this government reduced it to 80 cents. Then an act was brought down to make it 60 cents; then it was raised to 70 cents, and afterwards it was changed from 70 cents to 90 cents. Those hon. members who were in the house a few years ago will recall that Professor Hope, of the university of Saskatchewan, who carried on an investigation of farm prices, stated that when you took into consideration the interest charges which farmers have to pay, the price of wheat should be at least 95 cents a bushel at the point of production.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member will agree with me when I point out to him that, when he says there was an "act" brought down, it will be interpreted to mean that the house passed a bill which became an act. There was a bill before the house, but it did not become an act or legislation.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I accept the minister's correction; he is right.
The social credit party has on the order paper a resolution asking that at least one dollar a bushel be paid for wheat at the local elevator. I think that is only fair. The amount is not sufficient; it should be more, but at least that should be a basis to start upon. The Minister of Agriculture knows that that is not very much to give our farmers. I have under my hand a clipping from the Western Producer of January 21, 1943, which I will not take time to read, but which states that in the United States they are paying $1.13 a bushel, including some storage charges, at the local shipping point in the form of an advance. Note that that is only an advance, and the situation of their farmers bears no comparison to ours, who receive only 90 cents. It must be understood, too, that the 90 cents is for wheat at Fort William, and the freight in some districts is as high as 21 cents. That is not an average, but I understand it is even higher than that at some points. On everything western

The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
farmers sell they have to pay the freight; that is, it is taken out of the price they get; and to everything they buy, freight is added.
1 ask the minister how long our munitions industries would put up with conditions like that. He knows as well as I do that no industrialist in this country would consider for five minutes a set-up of that kind. They have told the government, and they told me when I visited their plants, that they intend to have the cost of production, and when they speak of the cost of production there is no fooling about it. All the freight charges, depreciation, insurance, and everything else one can think of-even the heating and lighting of the plant-are included, and on top of that they get a clear profit. Surely such discrimination is bound to end in disaster, and the government is directly responsible for such neglect and anything which may result from it.
I was interested in the minister's proposal to appeal to the government for increased prices, because I am sure he realizes that the farmers are not getting enough; otherwise he would not have said that he intended to appeal for an increase in prices.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not what I said.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Parity.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not say "prices".

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Increased revenue, was it-income? Well, that is money anyway. But the Minister of Agriculture knows he is knocking his head against a rock wall. Nobody knows that better than he does. He says, as reported in Hansard, at page 273:
I am going to make an appeal to the government-and 1 am sure it tvill be listened to-
I do not think he was serious in that.
-to give as high returns as possibly can be given for the commodities that are produced-
And this is the sticker:
-always keeping in mind the fact that funds must be found for other things as well as for paying for food.
Surely the Minister of Agriculture has not forgotten the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) not so long ago when he said that money was not going to stand in the way of production. He has not forgotten that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said that the only limit to our production will be the natural resources, the materials and the man-power. Yet the minister is trying, I was about to say, to put
a little propaganda across in his constituency, but he would not do that; he is holding up the bait, the carrot, in front of the farmers, and he says "I am going to appeal to the treasury for more money for you." But he knows quite well that he will not get it. He knows quite well that the Minister of Finance, speaking in Toronto a while ago, is reported to have said that Ontario farmers could not get adequate prices for their farm products without this causing disastrous inflation. If we stabilize farm prices, I would ask the minister, would that ruin our financial system? He knows better than that. Certainly it would not. If it does, it is a complete condemnation of our financial system.
Let me read for the guidance of the Minister of Agriculture what the Minister of Finance had to say in his budget speech. He said, as reported in Hansard, at page 845:
Receipts from the sale of farm products are reported to have reached a higher level in 1942 than in any year in the past two decades. Receipts from the sale of farm products are not equivalent to farm income. Farm costs have also risen but there is very evidence that farm incomes are at more remunerative levels than in any but the record years.
The Minister of Finance is definitely stating that the farmers do not need any more because they have a higher income than they ever had before. He continues:
Average weekly earnings of employed persons are at higher levels than they have been since the inflation boom following the war of 19141918. Thus there has been a far-reaching and important change in the distribution of income in the country. On the whole, the directions of the change have been desirable and the government has welcomed and facilitated it. The increases, by and large, have gone to those who needed them most.
He does not say that they have gone to agriculture. But this is the point:
But we have reached the point where the demands of some labour representatives and of some farm representatives cannot both be satisfied.
When you combine with this the statement which the Minister of Finance made in Toronto, I am afraid the Minister of Agriculture knows he will have no success.
I wanted to deal with the argument which the Minister of Agriculture put up in regard to parity prices, and in the little time which remains to me I wish to put on Hansard two statements on this matter. One is the definition of the Minister of Agriculture. This is what he said, as reported in Hansard, at page 272 as regards parity definition, and I quite agree with him:
Parity price is the price of the commodity which will give a purchasing power with respect
114S	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
to articles the farmer buys equivalent to the purchasing power of such commodity in the base period.
I do not think there is any argument on that definition. But I will now state, right after that, what is contained in the Searle Grain company's letter, their index with regard to parity prices:
The Searle index of the cost of things farmers buy (147 items) now stands at 153-7 (1913-14 equals 100). This means that these same things cost farmers of the west at the present time 53-7 per cent more than did similar items of the same quality in 1913-14. (These costs have risen 17-3 per cent since August, 1939.) The price of wheat is now 5-5 per cent higher than it was in 1913-14. The purchasing power of a bushel of wheat is now, therefore, only 68-6 pel cent of what it was in 1913-14.
