maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall conclude with these remarks, Mr. Speaker. The minister's definition of parity may be quite sound, but when you compare that with the Searle index, which has been carefully compiled for years past, even the hard-headedness of the Minister of Agriculture should permit him to see clearly that agriculture cannot continue producing under the cost of production. No industry, I do not care whether it is agriculture or munitions or anything else, can carry on indefinitely under the strain that agriculture is under without at least having its cost of production. As long as that condition exists you will have people leaving the farms, and this situation will be aggravated all the more. Therefore I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he get in touch with the Minister of Labour and come to an agreement on this man-power policy, and then get in touch with the Minister of Finance and arrange to give the farmer his cost of production plus a fair commission.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this budget has been received favourably by the people of Canada from one ocean to the other. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) stands high in the estimation of the Canadian people, and I believe he will stand even higher when the purport of this budget is thoroughly understood. His last words in his budget speech were, as reported at page 864 of Hansard:
Our soldiers, our sailors, or airmen "will do their part. They are well trained; they are well equipped; they are well led; their courage and devotion are beyond praise. But what they achieve, they cannot achieve alone. It must be shared by the farmer at his work, the mechanic

in the shop, the housewife in her home-in short, by every Canadian. Their achievements will be shared by each Canadian who, this year, and to the end of the war, carries out unswervingly, skilfully, relentlessly the watchwords of this budget: work and save.
I desire to bring to the attention of the house one or two problems which I believe are important at the present time. The output of the average Canadian worker in every sphere of industry is lessened by one factor which definitely can be reduced. I refer to ill health. The national industrial conference board in the United States estimates that the average worker loses about ten days a year on account of sickness. The "Personnel Journal" of November, 1943, estimated that the cost of these losses to the industry and the worker is around S70 a year.
Here in Canada we have the health league which has estimated that the average Canadian worker loses about nine days a year on account of sickness and industrial accidents, and about one-half day a year on account of occupational accidents. In Alberta the workmen's compensation board kept careful records for years of the causes of accidents, and then measures were taken to eliminate those causes. In that way the number of accidents has been reduced greatly. Macy's store in New York put into operation a sickness prevention programme which reduced absenteeism from 4-56 per cent in 1928 to 2-44 per cent in 1937. The cost of such a preventive programme was about $4 per worker.
Every war industry in Canada should have trained supervision, and causes of illness and accidents should be carefully recorded. In one plant absenteeism from ordinary colds was greatly reduced just by shutting off drafts. Nutrition should be supervised as well as rest periods, sanitation, hours of work, the ability of a worker to stand the stress and strain of his work, the causes of infection and all such matters. Every industry should arrange for periodic medical examinations because it is only in that way that men can be kept up to efficiency.
Modern research has reduced mortality and morbidity in typhoid fever, tuberculosis, appendicitis, scarlet fever, diphtheria and so on, and these diseases no longer are the dread things they were. The new sulfa drugs when given under supervision usually have a magical effect in lessening the virulence and shortening the duration of such things as tonsilitis, pneumonia, meningitis, gas gangrene and a long list of infectious troubles. Cancer has been the great scourge of the human race since the dawn of recorded history. If reported

The Budget-Mr. Gershaw
early, provided it is in an accessible place, X-ray, surgery or radium will generally bring about a cure.
In ending this portion of my remarks, I want to bring to the attention of the house one disease which at the present time might well be called the captain of the men of death. I refer to heart disease. Statistics do not always give a true picture, but one large life insurance company found that of 100,000 policyholders the death rate in 1922 from heart disease was 92-6, whereas in 1938 it had risen to 195-1. The three structures, the heart, the arteries and the kidneys, are subject to the same diseases and usually there is the same tragic end. Statistics have been assembled from 190 life insurance companies, and it is shown that from twenty-four to thirty-nine per cent of deaths are from heart trouble. The causes of heart trouble are given as overeating, overdrinking, lack of exercise, lack of rest, anxiety, noise, focal infection and the stress and strain of modern life. Undoubtedly each of these causes has some effect, although the precise effect has not been demonstrated. Therefore careful records should be kept to estimate the effect of each of these causes upon this very serious disease. I believe I am voicing the opinion of millions of men and women when I say that man's years upon this earth are far too few, and that the days of youth and usefulness pass all too rapidly. The frailties of age, the effects of disease come on before the fulfilment of many worthy tasks, and therefore the experience and skill and knowledge of many people are lost before their work is completed.
To turn now to another point, at this time there surely can be no argument against the statement that irrigation is very necessary in order to make agriculture as productive as it should be. It is nearly one hundred years since large irrigation schemes were started in the United States. During the last fifty years irrigation has been developed on a large scale. We can take the Grand Coulee scheme in the state of Washington where a million acres have been put under water. We have heard lately a good deal about India. Britain's greatest accomplishment in India was the building of irrigation schemes. The same applies to Egypt. The Arabs have a saying that "all sunshine makes a desert", and we know that where the sun shines almost continuously very little will grow unless other factors are brought into play. Long experience in southern Alberta has shown that the wet years come so seldom that it is not possible to depend upon moisture from the sky and the moisture must be obtained in some other way. The great areas of abandoned land and the
many deserted buildings indicating blighted hopes, impoverishment and despair amply prove this statement. In southern Alberta there are about half a million acres under water; there is sufficient water, and other conditions are favourable to irrigate two million acres. But it is impossible for private capital to carry out this work. It has been shown and is now accepted as a recognized principle that the initial capital cost of irrigation must largely come from public money. The Wilson report in the United States and the Ewing report in Canada amply and abundantly bear out this statement.
I desire to bring to the attention of the house the possibilities of just two of these schemes. The Canada land and irrigation scheme, including the Redcliff Ronalane scheme, was originally started by British capital. The original plan was to settle some 530,000 acres, of which 200,000 acres were irrigable. About 42,000 acres of this have been under water for a great many years in what is called the Vauxhall district, but the whole scheme has not been completed and the cost of completing it and bringing an additional 157,000 acres under cultivation would be only about $2,500,000, or from $17 to $18 an acre. The intake of this district is from the Bow river about thirty miles east of Calgary. There have been constructed a great artificial lake, reservoirs, and a canal about a hundred miles long. If we allow eighty acres of irrigated land and 160 acres of dry land for each settler, that district would make homes for 2,000 farmers, returned soldiers who have indicated that they wish to go farming, or farmers who could be moved from the marginal areas where they are subject to devastating drought and uncertainty.
The other scheme is one which has received unreservedly the recommendation of a committee appointed by this government. That committee reported in February, 1942. It consisted of Mr. Victor Meek, controller of the water and power bureau at Ottawa; Mr. George Spence, director of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act; and Mr. William Hunter of the accounts branch of the Department of Finance. A thorough investigation was made. It is the St. Mary and Milk river scheme. Those rivers run through both Canada and the United States, and the use of their waters is controlled by the joint international waterways commission. It is governed1 of course by treaty between Great Britain and the United States. This committee found that up to 1940 the United States people had constructed irrigation works sufficient to make full use of their share of the waters and also
The Budget-Mr. Gershaw

make full use of the unused Canadian share. Accordingly the committee recommended that the people of Canada should at once construct works to make beneficial use of this water because it would supply districts which now have not sufficient water, and would bring 345,000 acres under the ditch.
If the scheme were completed it would do much to balance production, so that we would not have so much wheat on our farms. It would be a great blessing to the farmers, to the community life of the district, and to the province and the whole dominion. About $15,000,000 would be required to bring 345,000 acres under irrigation. If the dominion put up $7,000,000 for the main reservoir and connecting canals and the provinces did the rest, it would cost them $8,000,000, part of which could be recovered.

speechtext:
Yes, at Spring Coulee
there is a reservoir site. It would take about three years to construct a reservoir. The scheme has been carefully gone over by engineers, is considered feasible in every way and would bring an enormous area under water.
The value of the live stock marketed in Alberta in 1941 amounted to $65,000,000, and the amount for grain, hay and seeds was only $62,500,000. Of every five hogs shipped to Great Britain in that year from Canada two came from Alberta. But a purely agricultural province is weak from an economic point of view. Irrigation would help to maintain the balance between industry and farming; sugar production could be proceeded with, as well as the canning of fruits and vegetables, the finishing of cattle instead of shipping them as feeders, the manufacture of commercial milk and so forth.
Some one may say, But the Canadian Pacific Railway Company spent millions there and never recovered it from the sale of land. That is true, but at the same time the Canadian Pacific Railway turned a great unproductive area into one where there are attractive and comfortable homes, thus greatly increasing the traffic over their road. Before they went in, when you drove over the prairie the air was dry; the cattle were thin; the vegetation was sparse and the dust rose in clouds. After irrigation was put in, you could see comfortable homes surrounded by grass, trees, shrubs and flowers. Small fruits could be grown; dairy products could be produced for the farmer and his family. Some will say that the provincial governments had to take over

the bonds of some of those districts, to the extent of $6,138,500. That is true, but it is also true that during the drought years, from 1931 to 1938, various governments spent not $6,000,000 but $51,000,000 for relief, none of which went to the irrigated districts. Under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act some $2,000,000 is collected through the one per cent tax on grain, but in the average year about $12,000,000 is spent under that legislation in connection with crop failures.
I bring these matters to the attention of the house because they are necessary to bear in mind if we are to have a maximum war effort and also for the welfare of the post-war period, which we now see so dimly and in so many colours. When the Titanic was sinking, a woman who had found a place in a lifeboat asked for three minutes in order to return to her cabin. There she saw her diamonds and jewels, but she reached past all those to grasp three oranges. Disaster had struck the Titanic and in a twinkling all values had changed. Now a storm is abroad in the world; values are being transformed, and the really precious, worth-while treasures are being appreciated and recognized.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seem to be a handy man to have around the house at times, when others are not prepared to go on. I want to say a few words about the budget, since I come from a city that is now the manufacturing, financial and industrial metropolis of Canada, which has surpassed the great city of Montreal and become the first city of the dominion, but before doing so I should like to refer to one other matter.
To-day I had occasion to ask one of the ministers a question, in a desire to encourage him in his work. Before the war, when the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) was Minister of National Defence, he brought down increased estimates covering the army and navy, and I was one of those who supported those estimates, because I saw the war coming. Those estimates were opposed by a great many hon. members on the other side of the house in 1937, 1938 and 1939. Since the beginning of the war I have believed in giving the government of the day all possible support, because they are the government and need encouragement. Our forces on land and sea and in the air have been magnificent. The history of courage has been gloriously rewritten in this war by those young Canadians who are serving in our armed forces and by the splendid showing of our navy.

The Budget-Mr. Church
During the session of 1937 I quoted Jeremiah for the benefit of some of our pacifists who believed in disarmament, and for some of my hon. friends from the province of Quebec. You will remember that he said, "Where are now your prophets that prophesied unto you, saying that the king of Babylon would not come against you, nor against this land?" Now we see what has happened since in the St. Lawrence. I sympathize with the hon. gentleman who is head of our department of naval services; he is not to blame, but I must say that a year ago I pointed out to him the condition that had been found by General de Gaulle around St. Pierre and Miquelon and in the gulf of St. Lawrence and the German submarines there. General de Gaulle warned Canada and the United States. Mr. Churchill happened to be in Washington at the time, in December, 1941, and the United States ambassador to Britain, Mr. Winant, cabled Washington in regard to certain occurrences in the gulf of St. Lawrence at St. Pierre and Miquelon. An attempt was made by Mr. Cordell Hull to prevent any joint statement being made in Canada in this connection, but Mr. Churchill sided with General de Gaulle, and Mr. Roosevelt also gave out a joint statement from the White House, overruling Mr. Hull. When Mr. Churchill was here he said that he believed ninety-five per cent of the people of France were with General de Gaulle and the free French movement.
At that time I also told the minister that we were in danger of being invaded; as the axis had submarines capable of crossing the Atlantic without refuelling; and all during the sessions of 1936, 1937, 1938 and 1939, until the war started, speaking from the place now occupied by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) I asked if we were to wait until the enemy came up the St. Lawrence by land, by sea and in the air and blew up the citadel before doing anything to defend ourselves. I referred to and gave a record of the submarine menace during the last war, and pointed out the grave danger of invasion which faced Canada at that time. I do not see very many of the newspaper columnists in the press gallery to-day. Perhaps I should first have asked their permission to speak, but I do not need any dictation from one or two of the newspaper columnists at times. Now we have the present situation on our hands in the St. Lawrence.
As you know sir, Mr. Lyttelton, the very able minister of production in Britain, spoke in New York on armistice day, November 11, 1942, and warned the United States and the 72537-73
allies of the very grave danger in connection with sinkings in the Atlantic and the approaches to North America. On February 24 I placed his full statement on Hansard. We are building ships, but as fast as they are built they are sunk. W'e are trying to get the people on our farms to produce more food, but the ships carrying that food are being sent to the bottom. Mr. Lyttelton referred in New York to that magnificent armada, consisting of 500 merchant ships and 350 warships to Morocco and Algiers by means of which the north African campaign was started and went on to say that this armada was escorted to North Africa by 120 escort ships. What has been the result? Those 120 escort ships cannot get back to the north Atlantic again, because they are needed in the Mediterranean. We have seen the magnificent victories achieved by General Montgomery, General Alexander and General Wavell, who has been called by the Russian generals at Stalingrad the greatest marvel in all military history. The other day in this house one hon. gentleman said that the advance achieved in North Africa had been an Anglo-American advance. It was not. The advance across Libya, a distance of 1,600 miles, was made by the 8th army under the command of General Montgomery, General Alexander and General Anderson. But an increased strain has been placed upon Atlantic shipping as a result of that north African armada, because, as you know, ships are still being sent, as they have been for over three years around the cape of Good Hope, a distance of ten thousand1 miles. The distance through the Mediterranean is only three thousand miles, so that you can see the great saving that would be made if that route could be kept open for food and munitions to the far east. The cost of that African armada was phenomenal, and it has had a great bearing on the number of sinkings that have taken place in the Atlantic, because the best part of it, the Anglo-American fleet, was formerly on north Atlantic war convoy work, and we are thus short, and the submarine menace is very grave, since we yet have not found' a solution to the new German U-boat that hunts at night in packs on the convoys and does not appear in daytime on the surface. The war is lost unless this is solved, and we cannot do anything until the allies regain command of the sea.
They noW have to defend the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Mediterranean. They are up against the axis fleet, and the air force of the axis powers. In addition to that, the whole question of submarine warfare had been

The Budget-Mr. Church

changed by Germany, who saw in it, with all the coast from Norway to Spain, a chance, with a new type of submarine, to win the war. No war is the same as the last one. Submarine warfare at the time of the last war nearly cost the allies the victory.
There have been references to sinkings in the St. Lawrence river, and off St. Pierre, twenty miles from Newfoundland, and this has become a problem. This is one of the main reasons why the allies should immediately try to get bases in Eire. Since the beginning of this war we did not have those bases. We had them in the last war, and the submarine menace, even with them there, nearly cost us the war. I say those bases should be immediately secured. They belong to our empire. The United States has asked for them, and so has Britain. Cities such as Cardiff, Coventry, Plymouth, Bristol and Birmingham have had their houses destroyed, and thousands of men, women and children have perished for lack of those bases, and our ships have to take the more dangerous north passage. I favour taking them, or the battle of the Atlantic may be lost, since we would have lost the last war without them.
Mr. Churchill made a statement with respect to U-boats on September 27, 1939. We had a submarine menace at the time of the last war, and we have a much more grave one in this war. Germany was quick to realize that she did not have a navy; she got one presented to her by the United States isolationist policy for two years, with the result that she developed new types of submarines, and we have had great loss of shipping in the Atlantic. Speaking on September 27, 1939, in the House of Commons, London, he said:
I see how much greater are the defences which we possess to-day in coping with the U-boat than we did in the first U-boat campaign twenty-five years ago. In those days there were moments when the problem seemed well nigh insoluble. Very often to hunt down a U-boat it was necessary to use a flotilla of fifteen or twenty vessels working together for a whole day on the vaguest indication. Now two destroyers or even one can maintain a prolonged and relentless pursuit.
This new equipment and the thorough training which the navy's light craft had had in this particular duty made it possible for a heavy toll to be taken of the U-boats from the start.
With regard to the present situation in the St. Lawrence of twenty or thirty,' or I know not how many sunk, may I say that I warned the minister a year ago about the situation at St. Pierre and Miquelon, and in reply he said that he would find out what the situation was.

The submarines that operated there last December were from the Canadian Atlantic. We have never heard a word as to St. Pierre and Miquelon from that day to this. General de Gaulle sent Admiral Muselier at. the request of the inhabitants to seize these islands. Mr. Hull pleaded the Monroe doctrine; Canada wavered. Mr. Churchill, standing here where our respected clerk, Doctor Beauchesne sits, said that the name of the Free French will be held and is being held in increasing respect by nine Frenchmen out of ten.
Rear Admiral H. G. Thursfield, one of the greatest authorities, is a man upon whom Mr. Churchill has been relying for advice. In an article in the February, 1943, issue of the National Review he discusses the U-boat menace and its solution. He points out that unless we solve the new U-boat situation in the Atlantic, the war is lost. There can be no doubt about that fact. This Admiral said:
There can be little doubt now that the German rape of Norway was a part of this plan, designed to provide the German navy with secure bases which were not dominated geographically by the British isles. The conquest of France fitted into the plan, too, as was shown by Hitler's contemptuous exemption of Vichieu France from occupation, and his seizure only of France's Atlantic coastal provinces. By June, 1940, German U-boats had at their disposal both the fjords of Norway and the French harbours of the bay of Biscay whence they could reach the open Atlantic without the necessity of running the gauntlet through the North sea or English channel. Moreover, German possession of the Danish, Dutch, Belgian and northern French coasts gave them more or less sheltered corridors by which their ships and U-boats could reach those advanced bases from Germany with a fair measure of safety and immunity from serious British interruption.
The article then goes on to refer to the number of ships which had been sunk. The statement was given out in Washington where Mr. Churchill said that we are not yet destroying U-boats as fast as new ones are being put into service by Germany. That was stated by Mr. Churchill last September, and repeated by a Washington naval authority last month, January, 1943. The result is that the number of U-boats is still increasing. The same Washington authority put the number operating in the Atlantic in the .middle of January, 1943, at one hundred, which would indicate at least some four hundred in service altogether. That figure is borne out by the experiences of a homeward bound allies Atlantic convoy early in December, the story of which was released a month later in January last. It was attacked over and over again throughout four days and nights, and no less than thirty-five actions were fought against U-boats, in the course of which two of them

Questions
were almost certainly sunk, and others damaged. The names of the ships were given out by Rear Admiral H. G. Thursfield in this article and also by the British and United States press. It was stated that the British destroyer, H.M.S. Fame and corvette H.M.S. Vervain, the Polish destroyer O.R.P. Burza and the Norwegian corvettes H.N.M.S. Eglantine, Rose and Potentilla all took part in the defence, as well as aircraft of the coastal command and of the United States Navy. Yet the convoy referred to did not escape without some loss.
The intensity of the attacks on this occasion clearly indicates that a large number of U-boats must have been engaged, a number quite compatible with the 100 throughout the Atlantic mentioned in Washington. That number is still growing, and will grow. Goebbels has forecast 1,000 U-boats in service this year, and indeed that fantastic figure might almost eventually be reached if we do not succeed in achieving a rate of destruction greater than the rate of new production by Germany. It will not suffice merely to beat off the attacks which U-boats make on convoys. The U-boats themselves must be destroyed at an increasing rate if the battle of the seas is to be won, and without the allies regaining command of the sea, the war cannot be won.
On motion of Mr. Church the debate was adjourned.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
